modules.title: Build once and keep the result

lessons.title: From a commit to production
lessons.intro: This course is about CI/CD: the automated path that takes a change from a developer's machine to the people who use the software. It is a reading course. Each module explains a few ideas, shows them as pipeline files, commands and diagrams, asks you to judge some situations, and ends with a short exercise and one possible answer. The ideas apply to any pipeline tool. So that the examples stay comparable, they are written for one tool, GitHub Actions, and deploy one running product, a small web service called tracker, to Microsoft Azure.

steps.title: The problem
steps.text:
Picture a team that releases by hand. Each developer works alone for weeks. At the end, everyone's work is combined, and it does not fit together. Then someone follows a long checklist to put the result on a server, late at night, and a step is missed.

Two things made that painful. The changes were **large**, so problems were found late and were hard to trace. And the release was **manual**, so it was slow, different every time, and frightening enough to be done rarely.

CI/CD attacks both. It makes changes small and checks each one at once, and it turns the release into a script that runs the same way every time.

steps.title: Three terms
steps.text:
- **Continuous integration** (CI) means every developer merges into one shared branch often, at least daily, and every change is built and tested automatically.
- **Continuous delivery** (CD) means every change that passes is packaged and proven ready to release. Releasing is one button, pressed by a person.
- **Continuous deployment** goes one step further: every change that passes is released automatically, with no button.

The two CDs share their initials, which causes confusion. The difference is only who starts the final step. Most teams practise continuous delivery, and automate the last step once they trust their checks.

steps.title: The pipeline
steps.text:
A **pipeline** is the series of automated steps a change passes through. It starts when the change is pushed and ends when the change is in production or has been rejected.

Each step is a **gate**. A change that fails a step goes no further, and its author is told. A change that passes moves on to a slower, more thorough step.

The pipeline is written in a file kept in the same repository as the code. That matters: the release process is reviewed, versioned and changed in the same way as the code it releases.

steps.title: Which practice?
steps.text: A team's pipeline builds and tests every change, packages it, and puts it on a staging server. A release manager reads the test results each afternoon and presses a button to release to production.

steps.title: Feedback is the product
steps.text:
The most useful thing a pipeline makes is not the release. It is **feedback**: a fast, trustworthy answer to "did my change break anything?"

The speed of that answer changes how people work. When it arrives in five minutes, the author still has the change in mind and fixes it at once. When it arrives the next morning, the author has moved on, three more changes have landed on top, and nobody is sure which one is at fault.

Two properties matter above all others.

- **Fast.** Minutes, not hours.
- **Trustworthy.** Green means it works, and red means it does not. A pipeline that fails at random teaches everyone to ignore it.

steps.title: The cost of a defect grows with time
steps.text:
The same mistake costs more the later it is found.

Found as you type, it costs seconds. Found by the pipeline, minutes. Found by a tester a week later, it costs a conversation, a search and a second release. Found by a customer, it costs trust as well.

So a good pipeline moves checks as early as it can. The cheap, fast ones run on every change. The slow, broad ones run later, on the few changes that got that far.

steps.title: A release day
steps.text: A team describes how it ships.

steps.title: Exercise: trace a change
steps.text:
Think of a project you know. Write down, in order, every step between a developer finishing a change and a user being able to use it. Include the waiting.

For each step note:

1. Is it done by a person or a machine?
2. Roughly how long does it take, including waiting for someone?
3. What happens if it fails?

Then mark the step that takes longest and the step most likely to be done wrongly.

steps.text:
A typical list for a small web service might read as below. The lengths are invented, and the pattern is common.

Two things stand out in lists like this. Most of the elapsed time is **waiting for a person**, not work. And the manual steps are the ones that fail in new ways each time.

The rest of this course goes through that list from top to bottom: checking changes, packaging them once, moving the package through environments, releasing it safely, and going back when it is wrong.

questions.prompt: What is the team practising?

choices.text: Continuous integration only
choices.feedback: They go further. Every passing change is packaged and placed where it is ready to release.

choices.text: Continuous delivery
choices.feedback: Every change is proven releasable, and a person decides when to release. That is delivery.

choices.text: Continuous deployment
choices.feedback: That would release every passing change with no button.

questions.prompt: What is the root of the team's trouble?

choices.text: Releases are large and rare
choices.feedback: Six weeks of changes go out together, so a failure could be caused by any of hundreds of changes, and the manual steps are practised only eight times a year. Smaller, more frequent releases shrink both problems.

choices.text: The release happens on a Friday
choices.feedback: Moving it to Tuesday changes when the pain happens. The release would still be large and manual.

choices.text: They need more testers
choices.feedback: More people checking a large batch by hand makes it slower, and the batch is still large.

lessons.title: Integrate small changes often
lessons.intro: Continuous integration is a habit before it is a tool. This module covers the habit: one shared branch that always works, small changes merged into it often, and automatic checks on every proposed change. The pipeline file comes in the next module.

steps.title: One branch that always works
steps.text:
Continuous integration rests on one agreement: there is a single shared branch, usually called `main`, and it is always in a state that could be released.

Everything else follows from protecting that. Nobody pushes to `main` directly. A change is proposed as a **pull request**, checked automatically, reviewed, and merged only when the checks pass.

The hosting service enforces the agreement with **branch protection**: rules that refuse a merge until named checks have passed and a reviewer has approved.

steps.title: Why small and often
steps.text:
A branch that lives for three weeks drifts away from `main`. Everyone else's work lands in the meantime. When the branch finally merges, the conflicts are large and the combined result has never been tested.

A branch that lives for a day barely drifts. Its conflicts are small, its review takes minutes, and if it breaks something there are only a few lines to suspect.

The work of integrating does not go away when it is postponed. It grows faster than the delay. Ten small merges cost far less than one merge ten times the size.

steps.title: Two ways to build a feature
steps.text: A feature needs about 1,500 lines of changes. One developer builds it on a branch for three weeks and opens one pull request. Another merges a 150-line piece every day or two, each one safe to release, with the unfinished feature hidden from users.

steps.title: Merging unfinished work safely
steps.text:
Merging daily raises a fair question: what about a feature that takes three weeks?

The answer is to separate **merging code** from **showing a feature**. Unfinished code can be in `main`, and in production, as long as users cannot reach it.

- Build the new thing beside the old one and switch over at the end.
- Put the new behaviour behind a **feature flag**, a setting that turns it on or off without a release. A later module covers flags.
- Merge the parts nobody can see first: the data structure, then the logic, then the screen.

Each merge must leave `main` working. It does not have to leave the feature finished.

steps.title: What a pull request check proves
steps.text:
A check on a pull request should answer one question: **if this is merged, will `main` still work?**

That is a statement about the combination, not about the branch alone. A branch can pass by itself and still break `main`, because `main` has moved since the branch was made.

Hosting services deal with this in two ways. They can test the merged result of the branch and the current `main`. And they can require the branch to be up to date before it merges. For busy repositories, a **merge queue** tests each change on top of the ones ahead of it and merges them in order.

steps.title: Green, merged, broken
steps.text: Two pull requests were opened on Monday from the same commit of `main`. Both passed every check. Both were merged on Tuesday. `main` now fails to build.

steps.title: When main breaks
steps.text:
Even with every guard, `main` will sometimes fail. What the team does next decides whether CI works.

A broken `main` blocks everybody: nobody can tell whether their own change is at fault, and nothing can be released. So it is the most urgent work there is.

- **Stop merging** on top of the break.
- **Revert first.** Undo the offending change to get back to green in minutes, then fix it properly on a branch. Debugging on `main` while the team waits is the slow way.
- **Close the gap.** Ask why the checks did not catch it, and add the missing check.

steps.title: Checks worth requiring
steps.text:
A required check must be fast and dependable, because every change waits for it.

| Check | Finds |
| --- | --- |
| Formatting and lint | Style problems and common mistakes, in seconds |
| Build or type check | Code that does not fit together |
| Unit tests | Logic that gives wrong answers |
| Dependency and secret scan | Known flaws in libraries, and keys committed by accident |

Slow and broad checks, such as a full end-to-end run, usually belong after the merge. The module on ordering checks explains where to draw the line.

steps.title: Exercise: rules for main
steps.text:
You are setting up a new repository for a team of six. Write the branch protection rules for `main`.

1. Who may push directly?
2. What must be true before a pull request can merge?
3. Which checks are required? Name three.
4. What should happen when a required check fails at random about one time in twenty?

steps.title: One possible answer
steps.text:
1. Nobody, including administrators. An exception that exists will be used on the worst possible day.
2. One approving review from someone other than the author, every required check green, and the branch up to date with `main`, or a merge queue.
3. Lint, build, and unit tests. They are fast and their failures are clear. A scan for committed secrets is a good fourth.
4. Treat it as a defect and fix or remove the test. A required check that fails at random teaches people to press "run again" without reading, and then it stops protecting anything. The module on speed returns to this.

questions.prompt: Which approach carries less risk, and why?

choices.text: The single pull request, because the feature is reviewed as a whole
choices.feedback: A 1,500-line review is rarely thorough, and the branch has had three weeks to drift from `main`.

choices.text: They are the same, since the same lines are written
choices.feedback: The lines are the same. What differs is how much is untested against `main` at any moment, and how hard a failure is to trace.

choices.text: The small pieces, because each merge is easy to review and to undo
choices.feedback: Each piece is checked against the current `main`, reviewed properly, and small enough to revert alone. Hiding the unfinished feature keeps `main` releasable throughout.

questions.prompt: How did two passing changes break `main`?

choices.text: Each was tested against Monday's `main`, not against the other
choices.feedback: One renamed a function and the other added a call to the old name. Each is correct alone. Requiring branches to be up to date, or a merge queue, tests the combination before it lands.

choices.text: One of the checks must have been skipped
choices.feedback: Both ran and both passed. They answered a question about an older `main`.

choices.text: The reviewers approved too quickly
choices.feedback: Neither change is wrong when read alone. Only the combination fails, and a machine has to check that.

lessons.title: Read a pipeline file
lessons.intro: A pipeline is described in a file. This module teaches you to read one. The examples use GitHub Actions, where a pipeline is called a workflow. Other tools use other words, and the same four ideas appear in all of them: what starts it, which machine runs it, what the units of work are, and how they are ordered.

steps.title: Where the file lives
steps.text:
In GitHub Actions a pipeline is a **workflow**: a YAML file in the folder `.github/workflows` of the repository. A repository can have several.

Because the file is in the repository, a change to the pipeline is a commit like any other. It is reviewed in a pull request, and each branch runs the version of the workflow that the branch contains.

Read the file below once from top to bottom before the next step takes it apart.

steps.title: Four levels
steps.text:
| Level | What it is | In the file |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Workflow** | The whole file. One automated process. | `name:` and everything under it |
| **Trigger** | The event that starts a run. | `on:` |
| **Job** | A group of steps that run on one machine. | Each entry under `jobs:` |
| **Step** | One command or one reusable action. | Each `-` under `steps:` |

A **run** is one execution of the workflow, started by one event. The run's page shows each job and each step with its output, and whether it passed.

steps.title: Runners
steps.text:
A job needs a machine to run on. That machine is a **runner**, and `runs-on` chooses which kind.

`ubuntu-latest` asks for a fresh Linux virtual machine provided by GitHub. It is created for the job and destroyed afterwards. An organization can also register its own machines, called self-hosted runners, when a job needs something special such as access to a private network.

The important property is that a hosted runner starts **empty**. Your code is not on it, and nothing is left over from the last run. That is why nearly every job begins by fetching the code, and why a job cannot rely on a file an earlier run created.

steps.title: Two kinds of step
steps.text:
A step does one of two things.

- `run:` executes a command in a shell on the runner, as you would type it in a terminal.
- `uses:` runs an **action**: a packaged piece of pipeline logic that someone published. `actions/checkout` fetches the repository. `actions/setup-node` installs a runtime.

An action is named with a version after `@`. Options are passed under `with:`.

Steps in a job run in order, on the same machine, and share its files. If a step fails, meaning its command exits with a code other than zero, the remaining steps are skipped and the job fails.

steps.title: An empty machine
steps.text:
A job has these steps, in this order, on a hosted runner.

```yaml
    steps:
      - run: npm ci
      - uses: actions/checkout@v5
      - run: npm test
```

steps.title: Jobs run apart
steps.text:
Each job gets its **own** runner. Two jobs share no files, and by default they run at the same time.

`needs:` makes one job wait for another. It also means the waiting job is skipped if the first one fails.

Because jobs share nothing, passing something from one to the next takes a deliberate step: a job **output** for a small value such as a version number, or an uploaded **artifact** for files. A later module covers artifacts.

steps.title: Values in the file
steps.text:
An expression in `${{ ... }}` is replaced with a value before the step runs. The values come from **contexts**.

| Context | Holds | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `github` | Facts about the run and its event | `github.sha`, `github.ref_name` |
| `env` | Environment variables set in the file | `env.NODE_VERSION` |
| `vars` | Settings stored in the repository | `vars.REGISTRY_NAME` |
| `secrets` | Secret values stored in the repository | `secrets.API_TOKEN` |
| `needs` | Outputs of jobs this job waits for | `needs.build.outputs.tag` |

`env:` can be set for the whole workflow, one job or one step. `if:` on a job or step runs it only when an expression is true.

steps.title: Two jobs, one mistake
steps.text: This workflow is meant to build the project and then run the tests against the build output. The `test` job fails with "dist folder not found".

steps.title: Exercise: read a workflow
steps.text:
Answer from the file below, without running it.

1. What starts it?
2. How many runners does one run use?
3. Which jobs can run at the same time?
4. If `lint` fails, which jobs run?
5. What does `deploy` know about the build, and how?

steps.title: One possible answer
steps.text:
1. A push to `main`.
2. Four, one for each job.
3. `lint` and `test`. Neither waits for anything.
4. `test` still runs, because it does not depend on `lint`. `build` needs both, so it is skipped, and `deploy` needs `build`, so it is skipped too.
5. Only the value `tag`, which `build` published as a job output and `deploy` reads through the `needs` context. It has none of the build's files.

questions.prompt: What happens?

choices.text: The first step fails, because the code is not on the runner yet
choices.feedback: A hosted runner starts empty. `npm ci` finds no `package.json`, exits with an error, and the later steps are skipped. The checkout has to come first.

choices.text: The steps are reordered so that the checkout runs first
choices.feedback: Steps run in the order written. Nothing reorders them.

choices.text: It works, because the runner keeps the code from the last run
choices.feedback: A hosted runner is created fresh for each job and destroyed afterwards.

questions.prompt: Why is the folder missing?

choices.text: The `build` job failed
choices.feedback: It passed. Its output was written to its own runner.

choices.text: `needs` runs the jobs in the wrong order
choices.feedback: `needs: build` does make `test` wait. Waiting does not copy any files.

choices.text: Each job has its own runner, and files are not shared between them
choices.feedback: The `dist` folder was created on the first runner, which was then destroyed. The files must be uploaded as an artifact and downloaded in the second job, or both parts must be steps of one job.

lessons.title: Decide when a pipeline runs
lessons.intro: A pipeline that runs at the wrong time is wasteful or dangerous. This module covers the events that start a workflow, how to narrow them, how to start one by hand, and how to stop two runs of the same pipeline from working against each other.

steps.title: Events
steps.text:
`on:` names the events that start a workflow. Four cover most needs.

| Event | Starts a run when | Typical use |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `pull_request` | A pull request is opened or gets new commits | Checks before merging |
| `push` | Commits arrive on a branch or a tag is pushed | Build and deploy after merging |
| `schedule` | A set time arrives | Nightly tests, dependency scans |
| `workflow_dispatch` | A person presses "Run workflow" | Production release, rollback |

A workflow can list several events. Each event that happens starts its own run.

steps.title: Narrowing an event
steps.text:
Most events take filters, so that a run starts only when it is useful.

- `branches:` limits a `push` to named branches. For a `pull_request` it names the branch being merged **into**.
- `tags:` starts a run when a matching tag is pushed, which is a common way to mark a release.
- `paths:` starts a run only when the changed files match a pattern. A change to the documentation need not rebuild the service.

Take care with `paths` on a required check. If the workflow does not start, the check never reports, and the pull request waits for it without end. Either leave required checks unfiltered or make sure something always reports a result.

steps.title: What runs?
steps.text:
A workflow has the trigger below. A developer pushes a commit to a branch named `fix-login` and has not opened a pull request yet.

```yaml
on:
  pull_request:
  push:
    branches: [main]
```

steps.title: Starting a run by hand
steps.text:
`workflow_dispatch` adds a "Run workflow" button, and the same can be done from the command line. It is the right trigger for anything a person should decide: releasing to production, rolling back, running a one-off job.

A manual workflow can declare **inputs**: values the person supplies when starting it. An input can be free text, a true-or-false box, or a choice from a fixed list.

Prefer a choice to free text whenever the valid values are known. A typed environment name can be mistyped. A list cannot.

steps.title: Schedules
steps.text:
`schedule` takes a cron expression: five fields for minute, hour, day of month, month and day of week. `0 6 * * 1-5` means 06:00 on Monday to Friday.

Three facts save trouble.

- Times are in **UTC**, not your local time.
- A scheduled run uses the workflow file on the **default branch** and may start several minutes late when the service is busy.
- Nobody is watching when it runs. A scheduled job that fails silently might as well not exist, so send its failures somewhere a person will see them.

Schedules suit work that is too slow for every change, such as a full end-to-end run, and work that depends on the outside world, such as checking dependencies for newly reported flaws.

steps.title: Two runs at once
steps.text:
Events can arrive faster than runs finish. Push three commits to a pull request in a minute and three runs start. Merge two pull requests in a minute and two deployments start, and the older may finish last and overwrite the newer.

`concurrency` prevents this. Runs that share a **group** name do not run at the same time.

- For **checks**, add `cancel-in-progress: true`. A new commit makes the old run's answer worthless, so cancel it and save the time.
- For **deployments**, leave cancelling off. A deployment stopped halfway can leave an environment in a mixed state. Let the running one finish, and the next waits its turn.

steps.title: The older one won
steps.text: A deploy workflow starts on every push to `main` and has no `concurrency` setting. Two changes were merged a minute apart. Afterwards, production is running the first change and not the second.

steps.title: Which code is this run using?
steps.text:
Each event decides which commit the workflow checks out, and it is not always the one you expect.

- `push` uses the commit that was pushed.
- `pull_request` uses a temporary **merge commit**: the pull request's branch combined with the current target branch. That is what makes the check answer "will `main` still work after merging?".
- `schedule` and `workflow_dispatch` use the newest commit on the default branch, unless a person picks another branch when starting it.

When a run's result surprises you, check which commit it ran on before anything else.

steps.title: Exercise: choose the triggers
steps.text:
Choose the trigger for each workflow, with any filter or concurrency setting it needs.

1. Lint and unit tests for every proposed change.
2. Build the service and deploy it to the development environment after each merge.
3. A full end-to-end test run that takes 50 minutes.
4. Release a chosen version to production.
5. Rebuild the documentation site, which lives in the `docs` folder.

steps.title: One possible answer
steps.text:
1. `pull_request`, with a concurrency group per pull request and `cancel-in-progress: true`.
2. `push` to `main`, with a concurrency group for the development environment and no cancelling.
3. `schedule`, nightly, with failures reported to the team. It is too slow to gate every change.
4. `workflow_dispatch` with an input for the version. A person chooses when, and the concurrency group is the production environment.
5. `push` to `main` with `paths: ['docs/**']`. It is not a required check, so the filter is safe.

questions.prompt: Does the workflow run?

choices.text: Yes, because of the `push` trigger
choices.feedback: The `push` trigger is limited to `main`. The commit went to `fix-login`.

choices.text: No, neither trigger matches yet
choices.feedback: The push is to a branch other than `main`, and there is no pull request. It runs once a pull request is opened, and again on each later push to that branch.

choices.text: Yes, twice
choices.feedback: Twice is what happens with an unfiltered `push` once a pull request is open: one run for each event.

questions.prompt: What went wrong?

choices.text: Both deployments ran at once, and the older one finished last
choices.feedback: Nothing made the second run wait for the first. A concurrency group for the environment would run them one at a time, in order.

choices.text: The second merge did not start a run
choices.feedback: Both runs started. The first was simply slower to finish.

choices.text: The trigger should have been `pull_request`
choices.feedback: That would deploy unmerged code. The trigger is right. The missing piece is ordering.

  # Every weekday at 06:00 UTC.

  group: ci-${{ github.ref }}
  cancel-in-progress: true

  10:01  merge B  -> run 2 starts   (fast: 3 minutes)

lessons.title: Order the checks
lessons.intro: A pipeline runs many checks. The order they run in decides how quickly a developer learns of a mistake and how much machine time is spent finding it. This module covers the kinds of check, the rule for ordering them, and what should run before a merge, after it, or overnight.

steps.title: Cheapest first
steps.text:
Every check has a cost, which is the time it takes, and a chance of failing. The rule for ordering them is simple: **run the checks that are cheap and likely to fail before the ones that are slow.**

A formatting check takes ten seconds. If it is going to fail, there is no reason to wait for a twenty-minute test run to finish first. Finding the cheap failure early is called **failing fast**.

The same rule says where to stop. Once a check has failed, the change will not be merged as it stands, so later stages need not run.

steps.title: Three levels of test
steps.text:
Tests differ in how much of the system they exercise.

| Level | Exercises | Speed | When it fails |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Unit** | One function or class, alone | Milliseconds each | You know exactly where |
| **Integration** | Several parts together, such as code with a real database | Seconds each | You know roughly where |
| **End-to-end** | The whole running system, through its user interface or API | Many seconds each | Something, somewhere |

The broader a test, the more it proves and the more it costs: it is slower, harder to diagnose, and more likely to fail for reasons unrelated to the change.

So aim for many unit tests, fewer integration tests, and a small number of end-to-end tests for the journeys that must never break. The shape is often drawn as a pyramid.

steps.title: Where does the slow suite go?
steps.text: A team has an end-to-end suite that takes 40 minutes and covers every screen. They want confidence, so they make it a required check on every pull request.

steps.title: Checks that are not tests
steps.text:
Some of the most valuable checks run no test at all.

- **Formatting and lint** catch style drift and common mistakes in seconds.
- **Type check or compile** proves the code fits together.
- **Dependency scan** compares your libraries against lists of known flaws.
- **Secret scan** looks for keys and passwords committed by accident.
- **Static analysis** searches the code for patterns that are often security bugs.
- **Build** proves that the artifact can actually be produced.

Most of these are fast and give clear answers, which makes them good early gates.

steps.title: In a row or side by side
steps.text:
Checks that do not depend on each other can run at the same time, as separate jobs. The pipeline then takes as long as its slowest job, not the sum of all of them.

`needs:` creates the stages. Jobs with no `needs` start at once. A job that needs them forms the next stage.

A **matrix** runs one job several times with different values, for example on three versions of a runtime or on two operating systems. Each combination is its own job on its own runner.

steps.title: Before the merge, after it, and overnight
steps.text:
Not every check belongs on the pull request. Sort them by speed and by how often they catch something.

| When | Budget | What runs |
| --- | --- | --- |
| On every pull request | About 10 minutes | Lint, build, unit tests, quick scans, a few key integration tests |
| After each merge to `main` | Up to 30 minutes | The full integration suite, building the artifact, deploying to a test environment, smoke tests |
| On a schedule | Hours | The full end-to-end suite, performance tests, deep scans |

A check that moves later still matters. Its failure must reach the team and be treated as a broken `main`. The only difference is that it no longer makes every change wait.

steps.title: An expensive order
steps.text: A pipeline runs its jobs one after another in this order. Most failed runs are caused by lint errors.

steps.title: A failure must be readable
steps.text:
A red pipeline is only useful if its author can tell what failed in under a minute.

- **Name every step** for what it checks, so that the summary reads as a list of results.
- **One concern per job.** "lint" failing says more than "checks" failing.
- **Keep the evidence.** Save test reports, screenshots and logs as files attached to the run, and do it even when the tests fail. That needs `if: always()`, because steps after a failure are skipped by default.
- **Put the cause first.** A step that fails should print what went wrong and what to do, not only a stack trace.

steps.title: Exercise: arrange a pipeline
steps.text:
A service has these checks. Arrange them into stages for the pull request, say which run side by side, and move anything that does not belong there.

| Check | Time |
| --- | --- |
| Lint | 20 s |
| Type check | 40 s |
| Unit tests | 3 min |
| Integration tests with a database | 6 min |
| Build the container image | 4 min |
| End-to-end tests | 35 min |
| Dependency scan | 1 min |
| Performance test | 25 min |

steps.title: One possible answer
steps.text:
**Pull request, stage 1, side by side:** lint, type check, dependency scan. All under a minute. Most mistakes stop here.

**Pull request, stage 2, side by side:** unit tests, integration tests, and the image build. They start only if stage 1 passed. The stage takes 6 minutes, the length of its slowest job.

**After the merge:** build and publish the image, deploy to a test environment, run a handful of end-to-end smoke tests.

**Nightly:** the full end-to-end suite and the performance test, with failures reported to the team.

The pull request gets its answer in about 7 minutes, against 75 if everything ran in a row.

questions.prompt: What is the most likely result?

choices.text: Fewer defects, with no real cost
choices.feedback: The cost is 40 minutes of waiting on every change, many times a day.

choices.text: The suite will be sped up to a few minutes
choices.feedback: Broad tests through a user interface are slow by nature. Wishing does not shorten them.

choices.text: Developers batch changes together and stop trusting the check
choices.feedback: A 40-minute wait pushes people to merge less often and in larger pieces, which is the opposite of integrating continuously. Broad suites also fail at random more often, so the check is rerun without being read. Keep a few key journeys on the pull request and run the rest after the merge or nightly.

questions.prompt: What does the order cost?

choices.text: Every lint error is reported 47 minutes late
choices.feedback: The cheapest, most frequent failure runs last, behind the two slowest jobs. Run lint first, and side by side with the other quick checks, and the same error is reported in 20 seconds.

choices.text: Nothing, since every check runs anyway
choices.feedback: They do all run when the change is good. When it is not, the order decides how long the author waits to find out.

choices.text: The end-to-end tests are less accurate
choices.feedback: Their accuracy is the same. What suffers is the wait for every other result.

order.code:

  | lint        |        | unit tests       |     | build artifact |
  | type check  | -----> | integration      | --> | deploy to test |
  | quick scans |        | tests            |     | smoke tests    |
  +-------------+        +------------------+     +----------------+
        |                        |                       |
       fail                     fail                    fail
        |                        |                       |
        +------------------------+-----------------------+--> stop

  Most bad changes stop in stage 1, after seconds.

lessons.title: Keep the pipeline fast
lessons.intro: A slow pipeline is paid for many times a day by everyone on the team. This module covers how to find where the time goes, how caching and parallel work shorten it, and what to do about tests that fail at random, which waste more time than any slow step.

steps.title: Measure before changing anything
steps.text:
Every run's page shows how long each job and step took. Read a few typical runs before deciding what to speed up. The slow part is often not the one people complain about.

The usual places time goes:

- **Downloading dependencies**, again, on a machine that starts empty.
- **Tests run one after another** that could run side by side.
- **Work that did not need to happen**, such as rebuilding parts the change did not touch.
- **Waiting**: for a free runner, or for a person.

Fix the largest one first, then measure again.

steps.title: Caching
steps.text:
A runner starts empty, so every run downloads the same dependencies. A **cache** saves a folder at the end of one run and restores it at the start of the next.

A cache is found by its **key**, a text label. The trick is to build the key from whatever decides the folder's contents. For dependencies that is the lock file, the file that lists the exact versions.

- Lock file unchanged: same key, the cache is restored, and the install takes seconds.
- Lock file changed: new key, nothing is found, the install runs in full, and the result is saved under the new key.

Many setup actions do this for you with one option, as the second half of the example shows.

steps.title: A key that never changes
steps.text:
A workflow caches its dependencies with the key below. A cache saved under a key is never overwritten. Three months later the lock file has changed many times.

```yaml
        key: npm-cache
```

steps.title: What a cache must never be
steps.text:
A cache is a shortcut, and nothing more. Two rules keep it harmless.

**The pipeline must give the same result with an empty cache.** If a run passes only because of something left in a cache, the pipeline is broken and merely looks green. Caches are deleted without notice when they are old or the storage is full.

**A cache is not a safe place.** Never put secrets in one. And remember who can write to it: a cache saved by one run may be restored by another, so do not let a build that will be released trust a cache that unreviewed code could have filled.

Things worth caching are downloads that are slow to fetch and fully determined by a file you can hash: dependencies, tool installations, and base layers of container images.

steps.title: Side by side
steps.text:
When tests are the slow part, split them. Divide the suite into groups, called **shards**, and run each on its own runner at the same time.

Four shards do not make a suite four times faster. Each shard still checks out the code and installs dependencies, and the groups are never perfectly even. Expect three times.

The price is machine time: the same work is spread over more runners, plus the repeated setup. That trade is usually worth it, because people's waiting time costs more than runners.

steps.title: Do less
steps.text:
The fastest step is one that does not run.

- **Skip what cannot be affected.** A change to the documentation does not need the test suite. Path filters, from the module on triggers, do this.
- **Cancel runs that no longer matter.** A new commit makes the old run's result useless. Concurrency groups do this.
- **Stop at the first failure when later results are worthless.** There is no point running stage 2 after stage 1 failed.
- **Fetch only what you need.** A checkout brings only the newest commit by default. Keep it that way unless a step needs the history.

steps.title: Flaky tests
steps.text:
A **flaky** test is one that sometimes passes and sometimes fails with no change to the code. It is the worst thing that can happen to a pipeline, because it destroys the meaning of red.

Once people learn that a failure might be nothing, they press "run again" without reading. From then on a real failure gets the same treatment.

The usual causes are few: a test that depends on the time or date, on the order tests run in, on data left by another test, on a real network service, or on something finishing within a fixed wait.

The policy that works: when a test is found to be flaky, take it out of the required set at once, record it, and fix or delete it within days. Automatic retries hide the problem and make every run slower.

steps.title: Just run it again
steps.text: A message in a team's chat, and the history of one test over two weeks.

steps.title: Exercise: shorten this pipeline
steps.text:
A pull request pipeline takes 19 minutes. Its one job has the steps below. Say what you would change, in order of benefit, and estimate the new time.

| Step | Time |
| --- | --- |
| Checkout | 10 s |
| Install dependencies | 3 min 30 s |
| Lint | 30 s |
| Unit tests | 4 min |
| Integration tests | 9 min |
| Build | 2 min |

steps.title: One possible answer
steps.text:
1. **Cache the dependencies**, keyed on the lock file. The install drops from 3.5 minutes to about 20 seconds on most runs.
2. **Split into jobs that run side by side:** lint, unit tests, integration tests, build. The pipeline now lasts as long as its slowest job plus setup: about 9.5 minutes.
3. **Shard the integration tests** in three. That job drops to about 4 minutes.
4. **Put lint in a first stage**, so a lint error is reported in under a minute and nothing else runs.

Result: about 5 minutes, from 19. The total machine time went **up**, because setup is repeated in each job. The cache keeps that repeat cheap, which is why it comes first.

questions.prompt: What does each run do now?

choices.text: Restores a cache that matches the current lock file
choices.feedback: The cache was saved once, three months ago, and never replaced.

choices.text: Restores the three-month-old cache, then downloads everything that has changed since
choices.feedback: The key always matches, so the old cache is always found and never updated. Each run fetches the growing difference again. A key built from a hash of the lock file would save a fresh cache whenever the dependencies change.

choices.text: Fails, because the cache is out of date
choices.feedback: A stale cache does not fail the run. It quietly stops saving time, which is why the problem goes unnoticed.

questions.prompt: What should the team do first?

choices.text: Remove the test from the required checks and record it to be fixed
choices.feedback: It fails about one run in four with no code change, so its result carries no information. Taking it out of the gate today restores the meaning of red. Then fix it or delete it.

choices.text: Add an automatic retry, three times
choices.feedback: That makes the check green and the problem invisible, at the cost of slower runs. The habit of ignoring failures remains.

choices.text: Keep rerunning, since it usually passes
choices.feedback: That is the habit that lets a real failure through. People have stopped reading what failed.

lessons.title: Build once and keep the result
lessons.intro: Between the checks and the deployment sits the thing that actually gets deployed. This module covers that thing, the artifact: why it is built exactly once, how to name it so that every build can be told apart, and where it is kept.

steps.title: What an artifact is
steps.text:
An **artifact** is the output of a build: the packaged form of the software that will run. Depending on the project it is a container image, a compiled program, a package for a library registry, or an archive of files for a web server.

The artifact is the unit that moves through the rest of the pipeline. Tests run against it. Environments receive it. Production runs it.

This course uses a container image as its artifact, since that is the common case for services. Nothing in this module depends on that choice.

steps.title: Build once
steps.text:
The central rule of delivery is: **build the artifact once, and deploy that same artifact everywhere.**

It is tempting to give each environment its own build step. Then staging and production run two different builds of the same source. They can differ, because a build has inputs beyond the source: the versions of dependencies that are available that day, the base image, the build tools on the runner.

If the artifact that passed your tests is not the artifact you release, the tests proved nothing about the release.

steps.title: The same commit, built twice
steps.text: On Monday the pipeline builds commit `3f2a9c8` and deploys it to staging, where it is tested all week. On Friday a production workflow checks out the same commit, builds it again, and deploys the result.

steps.title: Give every build a name
steps.text:
For one artifact to be carried through the pipeline, it needs a name that means exactly one build.

- The **commit identifier** is the simplest. Every build of `main` gets a tag such as `git-3f2a9c8`. It is unique and leads straight back to the source.
- A **version number** such as `1.5.0` is added when the project has releases that people talk about.

Whichever you use, the name is **permanent**. A tag is never moved to a different build. Names that move, such as `latest` or `stable`, cannot be used to say what is running or to go back to what was running before.

Compute the name once, early in the pipeline, and pass it to every later job.

steps.title: Where artifacts are kept
steps.text:
There are two kinds of storage, with different jobs.

| | Workflow artifacts | A registry |
| --- | --- | --- |
| What | Files attached to one run | A server made for storing versions of packages or images |
| Lives | Days, then deleted | As long as you decide |
| Use for | Passing files between jobs, keeping test reports | Anything that will be deployed |

The module on reading a pipeline file showed that jobs share no files. Uploading a workflow artifact in one job and downloading it in the next is how files cross that gap.

What gets deployed belongs in a registry, where it has a permanent name and every environment can fetch it. For container images on Azure, that is Azure Container Registry.

steps.title: Publishing an image
steps.text:
The job below is the heart of a delivery pipeline. It runs after the checks pass on `main`. It builds the image, names it after the commit, and pushes it to the registry.

From this point on, no later job builds anything. Each one takes the tag and uses the image that is already in the registry.

The sign-in step uses an identity for the pipeline with no stored password. The module on secrets explains how that works.

steps.title: Three builds
steps.text: A team's pipeline, summarized. Each deploy job contains its own build step.

steps.title: From a running system back to its source
steps.text:
Months from now someone will look at production and ask what exactly is running. Make that a one-step question.

- **Stamp the artifact.** Record the commit and build time inside it, as image labels or a small version file.
- **Expose it.** A `/version` address on the service that returns the commit turns "what is running?" into one request.
- **Record each deployment.** Which artifact, to which environment, when, started by whom. The pipeline's own history often serves.
- **Decide how long to keep things.** Keep every artifact that is or recently was in production, so that going back is possible. Clean up the rest on a schedule.

steps.title: Exercise: design the artifact flow
steps.text:
A service is built from `main` and runs in three environments: development, staging and production.

1. How many times is the image built for one commit that reaches production?
2. What is the image called?
3. Which job computes that name, and how do later jobs learn it?
4. A test report is produced by the integration tests. Where is it kept, and for how long?
5. Which images does the registry keep?

steps.title: One possible answer
steps.text:
1. Once.
2. `<registry>/tracker:git-<commit>`, with a version tag added to the same image when a release is cut.
3. The build job, as a job output. Deploy jobs read it through `needs`. A manual production workflow takes it as an input.
4. As a workflow artifact on the run, for a week or two. It is evidence about one run, not something to deploy.
5. Every image that reached staging or production in, say, the last 90 days, and the current production image always. Images that only ever reached development can go after a few days.

choices.text: Yes, as long as the build passes

lessons.title: Promote through environments
lessons.intro: An artifact does not go straight from the build to users. It passes through environments, each a more realistic copy of production, with a gate before the next. This module covers what each environment is for, how one artifact gets different settings in each, and what stands between staging and production.

steps.title: Why there are several
steps.text:
An **environment** is a complete place where the software runs: its servers, its database, its settings. Most teams have at least three.

| Environment | Purpose | Who uses it | Data |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Development** | See each merge running, minutes after it lands | Developers | Invented |
| **Staging** | A rehearsal for production, as like it as possible | Testers, the pipeline | Realistic, with nothing personal |
| **Production** | The real thing | Users | Real |

Each catches a kind of problem the one before cannot. Development shows that the pieces start together. Staging shows that the release procedure works and that the change survives realistic data and settings. Production is the only place that proves it works for users.

steps.title: The same artifact, different settings
steps.text:
The artifact is identical in every environment. What differs is **configuration**: the database address, the size of the servers, which outside services it talks to, and the secrets for each.

Configuration is kept outside the artifact and supplied by the environment. In GitHub Actions, a job names its environment, and that selects a set of variables and secrets stored under that environment's name.

So `vars.APP_NAME` can be `tracker-dev` in one job and `tracker-prod` in another, with no `if` in the workflow. The steps are the same. Only the environment name changes.

steps.title: Which value?
steps.text:
A repository has an environment named `staging` with a variable `APP_NAME` set to `tracker-staging`, and an environment named `production` with `APP_NAME` set to `tracker-prod`. A job is declared as below.

```yaml
  deploy:
    environment: staging
    steps:
      - run: echo "${{ vars.APP_NAME }}"
```

steps.title: Gates
steps.text:
A **gate** is a condition that must hold before the artifact moves on. Gates get stricter towards production.

- **Into development:** automatic. The checks passed and the change was merged.
- **Into staging:** automatic, once the deployment to development succeeded and its smoke tests passed.
- **Into production:** a deliberate decision.

An environment can carry **protection rules** that the pipeline cannot skip: named people who must approve, a waiting period, and a limit on which branches may deploy there. A job that names a protected environment pauses until the rules are satisfied.

The rules live on the environment, not in the workflow file. A change to the workflow cannot remove them.

steps.title: Promotion
steps.text:
Moving an artifact to the next environment is called **promotion**. Nothing is built. The deploy job is given the name of an image that already exists and points the environment at it.

A promotion workflow for production is usually started by hand, takes the image tag as its input, and names the protected `production` environment. It should refuse a tag that does not exist in the registry, so that a typing error fails at once.

Because promotion only changes which image an environment runs, it is fast, and it is the same action whether you are moving forward to a new version or back to an old one.

steps.title: Keep the environments alike
steps.text:
Staging is only worth having if a success there predicts a success in production. Every difference between them is a place for a surprise.

- **Same deployment steps.** If staging is deployed by the pipeline and production by hand, the production procedure is never rehearsed.
- **Same shape.** The same kinds of service and the same versions, described by the same infrastructure files. Staging can be smaller. It should not be different.
- **Realistic data.** A staging database with twelve rows will not reveal a query that is slow on twelve million. Use data of realistic size with personal details removed.
- **Configuration that differs only where it must.** Addresses and secrets differ. Feature settings and limits should not, unless there is a reason.

steps.title: Two procedures
steps.text: A team describes how each environment is deployed.

steps.title: Temporary environments
steps.text:
Some teams go further and create a short-lived environment for each pull request, often called a **preview** environment. A reviewer can open the running change before it is merged.

They are valuable for changes people need to see, such as a user interface. They also cost money while they exist and are easy to forget. If you use them, the pipeline that creates one must also destroy it when the pull request closes, and something should sweep up any that were missed.

steps.title: Exercise: gates for tracker
steps.text:
The tracker has development, staging and production environments. Decide the following.

1. What starts a deployment to each?
2. What must have passed before each?
3. Which protection rules does production have?
4. Which variables differ between environments, and which must not?
5. The team is five people. Who may approve a production deployment?

steps.title: One possible answer
steps.text:
1. Development: every merge to `main`. Staging: automatically, after development succeeds. Production: a person starts the promotion workflow and names the tag.
2. Development: the pull request checks and the image build. Staging: the deployment to development and its smoke tests. Production: the staging deployment and whatever fuller tests run there.
3. One required reviewer, and only the `main` branch may deploy.
4. Differ: the application name, the resource group, the database address, and every secret. Must not differ: the deployment steps, the image, and settings that change behaviour.
5. Any team member except the person who started the deployment. Two people then see every production release, and nobody waits on one named person.

lessons.title: Handle secrets and identity
lessons.intro: A deployment pipeline can change production. That makes it one of the most powerful things in an organization, and one of the most attractive to attack. This module covers how a pipeline gets the access it needs, why a stored key is the weakest way to give it, and how to keep untrusted code away from that access. It is general guidance and not a complete security standard. Where you work, your organization's own security policy and review decide what is required.

steps.title: What the pipeline holds
steps.text:
To deploy, a pipeline needs permission to push images, change servers and perhaps alter a database. Whoever controls what the pipeline runs can use those permissions.

So think of the pipeline as a privileged user, and ask the questions you would ask about any privileged user.

- **What can it reach?** As little as possible.
- **How does it prove who it is?** Preferably without a password that can be copied.
- **Who can tell it what to do?** Only reviewed code, on protected branches.

The rest of this module takes those three in turn.

steps.title: The secret store
steps.text:
A **secret** is any value that grants access: a password, a token, a private key. It never belongs in the workflow file or anywhere else in the repository, where everyone who can read the code can read it, for ever, in the history.

Pipeline platforms keep secrets in an encrypted store. A workflow refers to one by name, as `${{ secrets.NAME }}`, and the value is supplied when the job runs.

Secrets can be stored at three levels: for the organization, for one repository, or for one **environment**. Prefer the environment. A secret stored on the `production` environment can be read only by a job that names that environment, and such a job waits for the environment's approval rules.

The platform hides secret values in logs by replacing them with `***`. That is a safety net and not a guarantee, as the next question shows.

steps.title: Is it hidden?
steps.text:
A developer debugging a workflow adds this step, and reads the log afterwards.

```yaml
      - run: echo "${{ secrets.API_TOKEN }}" | base64
```

steps.title: Stored keys age badly
steps.text:
The traditional way to let a pipeline into a cloud account is to create a key there and save it as a secret. It works, and it has three lasting problems.

- **It does not expire.** A key created today is valid until someone remembers to remove it.
- **It can be copied.** Anyone or anything that reads it once has it for good, and using it from somewhere else looks just like the pipeline using it.
- **It has to be rotated by hand.** Replacing it means updating every place it is stored, so in practice it is rarely done.

A long-lived key is a standing risk that grows with time. The better answer is to store no key at all.

steps.title: Identity without a stored key
steps.text:
Modern pipelines can prove who they are without a password, using **federated identity**. It works in three moves.

1. When a job starts, the pipeline platform issues it a short-lived, signed **token** that states facts about the run: which repository, which branch, which environment.
2. The job presents that token to the cloud provider.
3. The cloud provider has been told in advance: "trust tokens from this platform that say *this repository* and *this environment*." If the token matches, it returns a short-lived access token.

Nothing secret is stored anywhere. There is nothing to leak and nothing to rotate, and the access lasts minutes. The identifiers in the workflow, such as the client and tenant identifiers, are names and not passwords.

In GitHub Actions a job asks for its token with `permissions: id-token: write`.

steps.title: Least privilege
steps.text:
Give each job the smallest access that lets it do its work.

- **The platform's own token.** Every job receives a token for the repository itself. Its default permissions can be broad. Set `permissions:` at the top of each workflow to the minimum, usually `contents: read`, and add more only on the job that needs it.
- **The cloud identity.** Give it rights over the one resource group it deploys to, not the whole subscription.
- **One identity for each environment.** The identity that deploys to development should be unable to touch production. Tie each to its environment in the trust rule, so that only an approved production job can obtain production access.

steps.title: Untrusted code
steps.text:
The pipeline runs whatever the repository tells it to. Three doors let in code that nobody on the team reviewed.

**Pull requests from outside.** A pull request from a fork contains a stranger's code and can change the tests the pipeline runs. For this reason such runs get no secrets and a read-only token. Do not work around that. In particular, the `pull_request_target` event runs with the base repository's secrets, so a workflow using it must never check out and run the pull request's code.

**Third-party actions.** An action runs inside your job with your job's access. A version tag such as `@v3` can be moved by its publisher to different code. Pin actions from outside your organization to a full commit identifier, and update them deliberately.

**Text that becomes code.** A branch name or a pull request title is chosen by its author. Inserted into a script with `${{ ... }}`, it is pasted in before the shell runs, and can end the command and start another. Pass such values through an environment variable, which the shell treats as data.

steps.title: A helpful comment step
steps.text: This workflow posts the title of each new pull request to the build log. It runs for pull requests from anyone.

steps.title: Exercise: review the access
steps.text:
Read the workflow below and list what you would change.

```yaml
name: Deploy
on: [push, pull_request_target]
jobs:
  deploy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v5
        with:
          ref: ${{ github.event.pull_request.head.sha }}
      - uses: some-user/azure-helper@main
        with:
          credentials: ${{ secrets.AZURE_OWNER_KEY }}
      - run: npm ci && npm run deploy
```

steps.title: One possible answer
steps.text:
1. **`pull_request_target` with a checkout of the pull request's code.** A stranger's code runs with the repository's secrets. This is the most serious fault. Deployment should start only from `push` to a protected branch or from a manual run.
2. **A stored owner key.** It is long-lived and can do anything in the subscription. Use federated identity, with rights over one resource group.
3. **An unpinned action from an unknown publisher,** at a branch name, given the key. Pin to a commit identifier, or use the cloud provider's own action.
4. **No `permissions:` block.** The job gets the default token permissions. Set them to the minimum.
5. **No `environment:`.** Nothing scopes the secret or asks for approval.
6. **`push` with no branch filter.** A push to any branch deploys.

After those changes the job can deploy from `main` only, to one resource group, with access that lasts minutes, after approval.

lessons.title: Deploy without downtime
lessons.intro: Deploying means replacing the running version with a new one while people are using it. This module covers three ways to do that without an outage, how to choose between them, and how the pipeline checks that a new version works before users are sent to it.

steps.title: The simple way, and its cost
steps.text:
The obvious deployment is: stop the old version, start the new one.

It has two faults. Between the stop and the start, nobody is served. And if the new version fails to start, the old one is already gone, so the outage lasts until someone gets either version running again.

Every better strategy follows one idea: **have the new version running and checked before the old one stops taking traffic.**

steps.title: Rolling
steps.text:
A service usually runs as several identical copies, called instances, behind a load balancer that spreads requests among them.

A **rolling** deployment replaces the instances a few at a time. Take one out of service, replace it with the new version, check that it is healthy, put it back, move to the next.

It needs no extra capacity beyond one spare instance, and it is the default on most platforms. Its important consequence is that **both versions serve users at the same time** for the length of the roll. A user may get the new version on one request and the old one on the next. The two versions must therefore work side by side, against the same database.

steps.title: Blue-green
steps.text:
A **blue-green** deployment keeps two complete copies of the environment. One, call it blue, serves all users. The new version is deployed to the other, green, which receives no user traffic.

Green can be tested at leisure, at its own address, with production's settings. When it is ready, traffic is switched from blue to green in one step.

Blue is left running the old version. If something is wrong, switching back is the same single step, and takes seconds.

On Azure App Service this is built in. An app has **deployment slots**, each a running copy with its own address. You deploy to a slot, check it, and **swap** it with the production slot.

steps.title: After the switch
steps.text: A team deploys version 1.5 to the idle slot, checks it, and swaps. Production now runs 1.5. Ten minutes later, error reports start to arrive.

steps.title: Canary
steps.text:
A **canary** release sends a small share of real traffic, perhaps 5 percent, to the new version while everyone else stays on the old one. The team compares the two: error rate, response time, anything the business measures.

If the new version looks healthy, its share is raised in steps until it has all the traffic. If it does not, the share goes back to zero, and only a few users saw the problem.

A canary is the only strategy that tests with real users at limited risk. It asks more of you: a way to split traffic, measurements good enough to tell the versions apart, and enough traffic for 5 percent to mean something.

steps.title: Choosing
steps.text:
| | Rolling | Blue-green | Canary |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Extra capacity | Little | A second copy | Little |
| Both versions live at once | Yes, during the roll | Only for a moment | Yes, for as long as you choose |
| Going back | Roll the old version out again | Switch back, in seconds | Set the share to zero |
| Tested before users see it | Each instance's health check | Fully, at its own address | No. Users are the test, a few at a time |
| Needs | A load balancer | Two environments or slots | Traffic splitting and good measurements |

For a small service on a platform with slots, blue-green is a strong default: simple to reason about, and quick to undo. Canary pays off when traffic is high and a bad release is costly.

steps.title: Check before the switch, and after
steps.text:
Whichever strategy you use, the pipeline should prove the new version works before giving it users.

- **A health endpoint.** The service answers at an address such as `/health` with success only when it has started and can reach what it depends on.
- **A smoke test.** After deploying to the idle slot, the pipeline calls the health endpoint and a few important pages. It retries for a short while, because a service takes time to start, and fails the job if they never succeed. No switch happens.
- **A check after the switch.** The same smoke test against the production address, and a look at the error rate for the next few minutes.

A deploy job that ends as soon as the platform accepts the new image has checked nothing. Accepting the command is not the same as the service running.

steps.title: Green, and down
steps.text: A deploy job and what happened next.

steps.title: Exercise: write the deploy job as a list
steps.text: The tracker runs on Azure App Service with a production slot and a second slot named `next`. Write, as a numbered list in plain words, the steps of the production deploy job. Include what makes it stop.

steps.title: One possible answer
steps.text:
1. Wait for approval, through the `production` environment.
2. Sign in to Azure with the production identity.
3. Check that the image tag exists in the registry. Stop if not.
4. Point the `next` slot at that image.
5. Smoke test the `next` slot at its own address, retrying for up to two minutes. **Stop if it never passes.** Production is untouched.
6. Swap `next` with production.
7. Smoke test the production address. **If it fails, swap back** and fail the job.
8. Record what was deployed, and what the previous image was.

The workflow below is the same list as code. After step 6 the old version sits in the `next` slot, which is what makes step 7's swap back possible.

questions.prompt: What is the fastest safe action?

choices.text: Fix the bug and deploy 1.5.1
choices.feedback: That takes a diagnosis, a fix, a review and a full pipeline run, while users see errors.

choices.text: Swap the slots again
choices.feedback: The previous version is still running in the other slot. Swapping back returns users to it in seconds. Then the cause can be found without pressure.

choices.text: Restart the production slot
choices.feedback: A restart brings back the same faulty version.

questions.prompt: What was missing from the job?

choices.text: A check that the new version actually works
choices.feedback: The job ended when the platform accepted the new image. It never asked the service anything. A smoke test against the health endpoint would have failed the job, and with a slot the broken version would never have received traffic.

choices.text: A longer wait before finishing
choices.feedback: Waiting without checking would only have delayed the same green tick.

choices.text: A second reviewer
choices.feedback: A reviewer approves the intent. No reviewer can see that a setting is missing at start-up.

deploy-production:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment: production                        # 1
    permissions: { id-token: write, contents: read }
    env:
      APP: ${{ vars.APP_NAME }}
      GROUP: ${{ vars.RESOURCE_GROUP }}
      IMAGE: ${{ vars.REGISTRY_NAME }}.azurecr.io/tracker
      TAG: ${{ inputs.tag }}
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v5
      - uses: azure/login@v3                       # 2
        with:
          client-id: ${{ vars.AZURE_CLIENT_ID }}
          tenant-id: ${{ vars.AZURE_TENANT_ID }}
          subscription-id: ${{ vars.AZURE_SUBSCRIPTION_ID }}

      - name: The image must exist                 # 3
        run: |
          az acr repository show \
            --name "${{ vars.REGISTRY_NAME }}" --image "tracker:$TAG"

      - name: Deploy to the idle slot              # 4
        run: |
          az webapp config container set --slot next \
            --name "$APP" --resource-group "$GROUP" \
            --container-image-name "$IMAGE:$TAG"

      - name: Smoke test the idle slot             # 5
        run: ./smoke-test.sh "https://$APP-next.azurewebsites.net"

      - name: Swap                                 # 6
        run: |
          az webapp deployment slot swap --slot next \
            --target-slot production \
            --name "$APP" --resource-group "$GROUP"

      - name: Smoke test production                # 7
        id: verify
        run: ./smoke-test.sh "https://$APP.azurewebsites.net"

      - name: Swap back if production is unhealthy
        if: failure() && steps.verify.conclusion == 'failure'
        run: |
          az webapp deployment slot swap --slot next \
            --target-slot production \
            --name "$APP" --resource-group "$GROUP"

lessons.title: Go back quickly
lessons.intro: Some releases will be bad, however good the checks. What matters then is how quickly users are back on something that works. This module covers going back, when to go forward instead, what cannot be undone, and how feature flags separate putting code in production from turning it on.

steps.title: Decide before the incident
steps.text:
During an incident, people are under pressure and short of information. That is the worst moment to work out how to undo a release, or to argue about whether to.

So decide in advance, and write it down.

- **How do we go back?** One command or one workflow, which has been tried.
- **Who may do it?** Anyone on call, with no approval needed to restore service.
- **When do we do it?** A simple rule, such as: if a release is suspected and the cause is not known within a few minutes, go back first.

Restoring service and finding the cause are separate jobs. Do the first one first.

steps.title: Going back is a deployment
steps.text:
A **rollback** is nothing special. It is a deployment of the artifact that was running before.

That is only possible because of earlier decisions in this course. The previous artifact still exists in the registry, under a name that never moved. The pipeline recorded which one it was. And promotion only points an environment at an existing image, so the same workflow goes backwards as easily as forwards.

With blue-green slots it is faster still, for a short while after a release: the old version is still running in the other slot, and a swap restores it.

steps.title: Back or forward
steps.text:
The alternative to going back is to **roll forward**: fix the fault and release again.

| | Roll back | Roll forward |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Time to restore | Seconds to minutes | A fix, a review and a full pipeline run |
| Needs the cause to be known | No | Yes |
| Risk | Low: the old version is known to work | A hurried fix can add a second fault |
| When it is the only option | | When going back is impossible, usually because of data |

Going back is the default. Go forward when the fix is a line or two and certain, or when the old version can no longer run.

steps.title: Five percent
steps.text: Twelve minutes after a release, 5 percent of requests are failing. The team suspects the release and has two theories about the cause.

steps.title: What cannot be undone
steps.text:
Replacing the code does not reverse what the code already did.

- **Data it wrote or changed.** Rows saved in a new format are still there when the old version returns, and it may not understand them.
- **Changes to the database's structure.** If the release removed a column, the old version that reads it cannot run.
- **Messages it sent.** Emails, notifications to other systems and payments have left the building.

This is why a rollback has to be planned when the change is designed, not when it fails. Ask of every change: if this is rolled back after running for an hour, will the old version work with what it left behind? The next module covers the hardest case, the database.

steps.title: Deploying is not releasing
steps.text:
So far, putting code into production and showing it to users have been one event. They need not be.

A **feature flag** is a setting, read while the program runs, that decides whether a piece of behaviour is on. The code for a new feature is deployed with its flag off. Nobody sees it. Later the flag is turned on, with no deployment.

This gives three things.

- **Small merges.** Unfinished work can be merged and deployed safely, as the module on integrating promised.
- **A gradual release.** Turn the feature on for staff, then for 5 percent of users, then for everyone.
- **An off switch.** If the feature misbehaves, turn the flag off. That takes seconds and needs no rollback.

steps.title: Flags have a cost
steps.text:
Every flag is a fork in the code. With it on and with it off are two programs, and both must work. Ten flags can combine in a thousand ways, and nobody tests them all.

Treat a release flag as temporary scaffolding.

- **Give each flag an owner and a removal date** when it is created.
- **Remove it once the feature is fully on.** Deleting the flag and the old code path is part of finishing the feature.
- **Keep a list.** A flag nobody remembers is a setting that can change behaviour by accident.
- **Do not confuse kinds.** A flag that hides unfinished work is short-lived. A permanent setting, such as a limit that differs by customer, is configuration and should be managed as such.

steps.title: Exercise: write the page
steps.text:
Write the one-page instructions for a bad release of the tracker. It runs on slots, and images are tagged by commit. Cover:

1. How someone decides that going back is right.
2. The exact action in the first ten minutes after a release.
3. The exact action a day later, when the other slot has been reused.
4. What to check afterwards.
5. What must be true of every release for this page to work.

steps.title: One possible answer
steps.text:
1. **Decide.** If errors or complaints rise after a release and the cause is not known within five minutes, go back. No approval is needed.
2. **Within minutes of the release.** Run the rollback workflow with `mode: swap`. It swaps the slots, which restores the previous version in seconds.
3. **Later.** Run it with `mode: tag` and the previous image tag, taken from the deployment record. It deploys that image through the usual slot, smoke test and swap.
4. **Afterwards.** Check the health endpoint and the error rate. Tell the team which version is now running. Then find the cause, with production stable.
5. **Conditions.** Every release keeps its image. Every release records the previous tag. No release makes a database change the previous version cannot run with.

The fifth point is the one teams discover too late, and it is the subject of the next module.

questions.prompt: What should they do first?

choices.text: Roll back, then investigate
choices.feedback: Users are affected now, and the cause is not known. Going back restores service in a minute or two and removes the pressure. If the errors continue, the release was not the cause, and that is learned quickly too.

choices.text: Test both theories in production
choices.feedback: That keeps users on a failing version for as long as the investigation takes.

choices.text: Write a fix for the likelier theory and release it
choices.feedback: A hurried fix for an unconfirmed cause may not help, and can add a second fault.

questions.prompt: What habit would have prevented this?

choices.text: Using fewer flags for new features
choices.feedback: Flags for new work were not the cause. A flag that should have been deleted years ago was.

choices.text: Testing every combination of flags
choices.feedback: With 140 flags there are more combinations than could ever be tested.

choices.text: Removing each flag once its feature is fully on
choices.feedback: The flag had been on for everyone for three years and guarded code nobody had run since. Deleting it, and the old path, when the rollout finished would have left nothing to switch by mistake.
