# .github/workflows/rollback-production.yml
name: Roll back production

on:
  workflow_dispatch:
    inputs:
      mode:
        description: swap = undo the last release, tag = deploy an image
        type: choice
        options: [swap, tag]
        required: true
      tag:
        description: Image tag (only for mode "tag")
        type: string

concurrency:
  group: deploy-production
  cancel-in-progress: false

jobs:
  rollback:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment: production-rollback   # no approval: restore first
    permissions: { id-token: write, contents: read }
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v5
      - uses: azure/login@v3
        with:
          client-id: ${{ vars.AZURE_CLIENT_ID }}
          tenant-id: ${{ vars.AZURE_TENANT_ID }}
          subscription-id: ${{ vars.AZURE_SUBSCRIPTION_ID }}

      - name: Swap the slots back
        if: inputs.mode == 'swap'
        run: |
          az webapp deployment slot swap --slot next \
            --target-slot production \
            --name "${{ vars.APP_NAME }}" \
            --resource-group "${{ vars.RESOURCE_GROUP }}"

      # mode "tag" would call the same deploy steps as a normal release.

      - name: Check production
        env:
          APP: ${{ vars.APP_NAME }}
        run: ./smoke-test.sh "https://$APP.azurewebsites.net"

lessons.title: Change the database safely
lessons.intro: Code can be replaced in seconds and put back just as fast. A database cannot: it holds the only copy of the data, and its structure is shared by every version of the code that is running. This module covers how to change a database's structure through a pipeline so that a deployment, and a rollback, both keep working.

steps.title: Why the database is different
steps.text:
Three facts set the database apart from everything else in a release.

- **There is one.** You cannot keep the old database beside the new one and switch between them, as you can with code.
- **Old and new code share it.** During a rolling deployment, or the moment of a swap, both versions are running against the same tables.
- **Going back does not undo it.** A rollback replaces the code. The database stays as the new version left it.

So a change to the database has to work with the version of the code before it **and** the version after it. That one requirement drives everything in this module.

steps.title: Migrations
steps.text:
A **migration** is a small script that changes the database's structure: add a table, add a column, create an index. Migrations are kept in the repository, numbered in order.

A migration tool applies them. It keeps a table in the database that lists which migrations have already run, and runs only the new ones, in order, each exactly once.

Two rules make this dependable.

- **Never edit a migration that has been applied anywhere.** Write a new one. An edited script has already run in some environments in its old form, and they will never match again.
- **Only the pipeline runs migrations.** A change typed into production by hand exists in one environment and in nobody's records.

steps.title: The change that breaks
steps.text:
Suppose the column `owner` on the tasks table should be called `assignee`. The obvious release renames the column and updates the code to match.

Follow it through a deployment. The migration runs first and the column is renamed. For the next minute, instances of the old code are still serving users. They ask for `owner`, which no longer exists, and every such request fails.

Now suppose the new version has a fault and is rolled back. The old code returns for good, still asking for `owner`. The rollback has made things worse.

A rename, a removal, or a change of type in a single step is a **breaking** change to the database, for the same reason it would be in an API: something that depends on the old shape is still running.

steps.title: One release
steps.text: A release contains a migration that drops the column `legacy_code`, and code that no longer reads it. The service runs four instances and deploys by rolling.

steps.title: Expand, then contract
steps.text:
The safe pattern splits one breaking change into several releases, none of which breaks anything.

1. **Expand.** Add the new structure beside the old. Nothing uses it yet, so nothing can break.
2. **Write both.** Release code that writes to the old and the new, and still reads the old.
3. **Backfill.** Copy existing data from the old structure to the new, in small batches.
4. **Read new.** Release code that reads the new structure. It still writes both, so going back to step 2's code is safe.
5. **Stop writing old.** Release code that uses only the new.
6. **Contract.** Once nothing has used the old structure for a while, remove it.

Each step is its own release, and after each one the previous version of the code still runs. It is slower than one release. It is also the only way that never has a moment where running code and the database disagree.

steps.title: Rules for a safe migration
steps.text:
- **Add, do not change.** New tables and new columns are safe. Renames, removals and type changes go through expand and contract.
- **New columns must be optional.** Allow them to be empty, or give them a default. The old code does not know the column exists and will not fill it in.
- **Removal waits a release.** Drop something only after a release in which no code touches it has been running without trouble.
- **Mind the size.** A change that is instant on a small table can lock a large one for minutes, and requests queue behind it. Try migrations against a copy of realistic size.
- **Move data in batches.** One statement that updates ten million rows holds its locks until it finishes. A loop over a few thousand at a time does not.

steps.title: Migrations in the pipeline
steps.text:
- **Run them as their own step, before the new code.** With additive migrations the old code keeps working after the step, so the order is always safe.
- **Run them once.** Several instances starting together must not all try to migrate. A separate job, or the tool's own lock, ensures a single run.
- **Run them everywhere the same way.** Staging gets the same migrations by the same step, first, on realistic data. That is where a slow or failing one is found.
- **Do not rely on "down" scripts.** A script that reverses a migration cannot bring back removed data. Prefer changes that never need reversing, and fix problems with a new migration.
- **Have a backup, and have restored one.** A backup that has never been restored is a hope. Practise the restore.

steps.title: Exercise: split a column
steps.text:
The `users` table has one column, `full_name`. The product now needs `first_name` and `last_name` separately. The service deploys by rolling and must be able to roll back one release at any point.

Plan the releases. For each, say what the migration does and what the code does.

steps.title: One possible answer
steps.text:
1. **Release 1, expand.** Migration: add `first_name` and `last_name`, both allowed to be empty. Code: unchanged.
2. **Release 2, write both.** Code: when a name is saved, write `full_name` and also the two new columns. Reads still use `full_name`.
3. **Backfill.** A batch job fills the two new columns for existing rows. Names that cannot be split cleanly are listed for a person to check.
4. **Release 3, read new.** Code: read the two new columns, still write all three. Rolling back to release 2 is safe, because `full_name` is still kept up to date.
5. **Release 4, stop writing old.** Code: `full_name` is no longer written or read.
6. **Release 5, contract.** Migration: drop `full_name`, after release 4 has run without trouble.

Five releases for one rename looks like a lot. Each is tiny and safe, and none of them can cause an outage.

questions.prompt: What happens during the deployment?

choices.text: Nothing, the new code does not read the column
choices.feedback: The new code does not. The old code is still running on some instances while the roll is in progress.

choices.text: Requests served by the old instances fail until the roll finishes
choices.feedback: The migration removes the column while old instances are still reading it. And if the release is rolled back, the old code cannot run at all. The column should be dropped in a later release, after one in which no code reads it.

choices.text: The migration waits until every instance is updated
choices.feedback: Migrations run before the new code starts. Nothing makes them wait for the old code to stop.

questions.prompt: What is wrong with this pull request?

choices.text: It renames a column and changes the code in a single release
choices.feedback: Between the migration and the end of the deployment, old code asks for `owner_id` and fails. A rollback would fail for the same reason. It needs the expand and contract steps: add the new column, write both, backfill, read new, then remove the old.

choices.text: The migration should be edited into an earlier one
choices.feedback: A migration that has already run is never edited. A new one is correct.

choices.text: Nothing, the code and the database match
choices.feedback: They match once the release is complete. During it, and after a rollback, they do not.

lessons.title: Reuse pipeline code
lessons.intro: One good pipeline is soon copied to the next repository, and the next. A year later there are thirty slightly different copies and a flaw to fix in each. This module covers the two ways to share pipeline logic properly, how to version what is shared, and the price of putting it all in one place.

steps.title: Copies drift
steps.text:
Copying a working workflow into a new repository is the fastest way to start. It is also a fork. From that moment the two files change separately.

Then a problem is found in the deploy steps: a missing check, an action that needs updating, a security fix. It has to be made in every copy, by hand. Some are missed. Some copies have been edited and no longer match the fix.

Shared pipeline logic should be written once, kept in one place, and **called** from each repository. Pipeline tools provide two shapes for this, at two different sizes.

steps.title: Two sizes of reuse
steps.text:
| | Composite action | Reusable workflow |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Replaces | A few **steps** inside a job | One or more whole **jobs** |
| Called from | A step, with `uses:` | A job, with `uses:` |
| Runs on | The calling job's runner | Its own runners |
| Can set an environment, approvals, permissions | No, the calling job does | Yes |
| Good for | "Sign in and push an image", "set up the tools" | "The standard deployment", "the standard checks" |

Choose by what you are sharing. A handful of commands that appear in the middle of different jobs is a composite action. A complete procedure with its own gates is a reusable workflow.

steps.title: A composite action
steps.text:
A **composite action** is a folder with a file named `action.yml`. The file declares inputs and lists steps, written as in any job.

It can live in the same repository, and is then called by its path. Or it can live in a shared repository, and is called by that repository's name, the folder, and a version.

Two details differ from an ordinary job. Every `run` step must name its `shell`. And the action runs inside the caller's job, so it sees that job's files and has that job's access.

steps.title: A reusable workflow
steps.text:
A **reusable workflow** is an ordinary workflow file whose trigger is `workflow_call`. It declares the inputs and secrets it expects.

Another workflow calls it from a job. That job has no steps of its own. It names the file with `uses:`, passes values under `with:`, and passes secrets under `secrets:`.

The called workflow brings its own jobs, runners, environment and permissions. That makes it the right shape for a deployment: the approval gate and the smoke tests are part of what is shared, so no repository can leave them out.

steps.title: Which shape?
steps.text: Twelve repositories each have a build job. The jobs differ, because the projects are built differently. In the middle of each are the same four steps: sign in to the cloud, sign in to the registry, build the image, push it.

steps.title: Version what you share
steps.text:
Shared code is a dependency of every repository that calls it. Treat it as one.

A caller names a version after the `@`: a branch, a tag, or a commit identifier.

- **A branch**, such as `@main`, means every caller picks up every change the moment it is merged. A fix reaches everyone at once. So does a mistake.
- **A tag**, such as `@v2`, means callers change when they choose to. A fix must be adopted repository by repository.
- **A commit identifier** cannot change at all.

A common arrangement: release shared code with version tags, and keep a moving major tag such as `v2` that receives only compatible fixes. A breaking change gets `v3`, and callers move when ready. This is the versioning discipline of any library, applied to pipelines.

steps.title: The price of one place
steps.text:
Centralizing is a trade, and it is worth seeing both sides.

**What you gain.** One fix reaches every repository. Every team gets the same gates. A new repository has a full pipeline in ten lines.

**What you pay.** One mistake can stop every team's deployments. Someone has to own the shared code, review changes to it, and answer questions. And teams lose some freedom: the shared workflow does things one way.

Three habits keep the price down.

- **Keep the interface small.** A few clear inputs. Every extra option is a thing to support for ever.
- **Test the shared code.** Give it a sample repository that calls it on every change.
- **Write it down.** Inputs, what it does, how to move between versions.

steps.title: Everything stopped at once
steps.text: A message to an engineering channel on a Tuesday afternoon.

steps.title: Exercise: what to share
steps.text:
An organization has twenty services. Each repository has its own copies of the items below. For each, say whether you would share it, in which shape, and why.

1. The six steps that sign in to Azure and push an image.
2. The production deployment: approval, deploy to a slot, smoke test, swap.
3. The unit test command, which is different in every repository.
4. The step that posts a message to chat when a deployment finishes.
5. The list of required checks on pull requests.

steps.title: One possible answer
steps.text:
1. **Composite action.** The same steps, used inside build jobs that otherwise differ.
2. **Reusable workflow.** It is a whole procedure with its own environment and gates, and sharing it guarantees no service skips the smoke test.
3. **Do not share.** It differs everywhere. A shared wrapper would need an option for every project and help nobody.
4. **Composite action.** One small step with a couple of inputs.
5. **Not pipeline code at all.** It is a repository setting. Many platforms let an organization apply such rules to many repositories at once, which is the right tool.

The test for sharing is whether the logic is truly the same. Sharing things that only look alike produces an abstraction with twenty special cases.

questions.prompt: How should the four steps be shared?

choices.text: As a composite action
choices.feedback: They are steps that run inside a larger job, on that job's runner, among steps that differ from project to project. That is what a composite action is for.

choices.text: As a reusable workflow
choices.feedback: A reusable workflow replaces whole jobs on its own runners. These steps need the files that the surrounding build steps produced on the same machine.

choices.text: By copying them, since they are short
choices.feedback: Four steps in twelve places is forty-eight chances to miss the next fix.

questions.prompt: What would have limited the damage?

choices.text: Not sharing the deploy workflow
choices.feedback: Then the same change would be needed in thirty files by hand. Sharing is right. How callers follow changes is the issue.

choices.text: Callers pinned to a version tag, and a test repository for the shared workflow
choices.feedback: With `@main`, an unreleased change reached thirty repositories the instant it merged. With tags, it would have reached none until released, and a sample caller run on every change would have caught the missing input first.

choices.text: A second approval on production deployments
choices.feedback: The deployments never reached the approval step. The workflow file itself was invalid for every caller.

lessons.title: Describe infrastructure as code
lessons.intro: The pipeline deploys to servers, databases and networks that had to come from somewhere. This module covers describing that infrastructure in files, previewing a change before making it, keeping environments alike, and what happens when someone changes things by hand. The examples use Bicep, the description language for Azure. Other tools, such as Terraform, follow the same ideas.

steps.title: Clicks do not repeat
steps.text:
An environment built by clicking through a cloud portal has three problems.

- **Nobody knows exactly what it is.** The settings are whatever was clicked, months ago, by someone who may have left.
- **It cannot be made again.** A second environment built the same way will differ in small ways, and those are the ways that matter.
- **Changes leave no trace.** There is no review beforehand and no history afterwards.

**Infrastructure as code** means the environment is described in text files, kept in a repository, and created by a tool that reads them. The description gets everything that code gets: review, history, and a pipeline.

steps.title: Describe, do not instruct
steps.text:
There are two ways to write down infrastructure.

A **script** lists actions: create a server, then create a database, then connect them. Run it twice and it tries to create everything twice.

A **declarative** file states what should exist: there is a server like this and a database like that. A tool compares the description with what is really there and makes only the changes needed to close the gap.

That gives the property that matters most. Applying the same description twice changes nothing the second time. It is safe to run on every merge.

The file below describes an App Service plan and a web app. It takes the environment's name as a parameter and builds every other name from it.

steps.title: Apply it again
steps.text: A description of an environment is applied by the pipeline, and everything is created. Nothing in the file changes. The pipeline applies it again the next day.

steps.title: Preview before applying
steps.text:
Because the tool works out the difference itself, it can show that difference **without making it**. On Azure the command is `what-if`. Terraform calls it `plan`.

The preview lists what would be created, modified and deleted. It is the most important safety step in infrastructure work, because the file alone does not show what will happen. A one-word change can mean "alter a setting" or "delete this database and make a new, empty one".

Put the preview where the reviewer will see it: run it on the pull request and attach the output. Reviewing an infrastructure change means reading the preview, not only the diff.

steps.title: One description, several environments
steps.text:
The module on environments asked that staging and production be alike. Infrastructure as code is how.

Write **one** description. Give it parameters for the few things that should differ: the name, the size, the number of instances. Keep a small parameter file for each environment.

Staging and production are then built from the same file. A setting cannot be added to production and forgotten in staging, because there is nowhere to write it that applies to only one, except in a parameter that everyone can see.

steps.title: Drift
steps.text:
**Drift** is the gap that opens when someone changes real infrastructure without changing the description. A size is raised in the portal during an incident. A firewall rule is added by hand to test something and left.

Now the file is wrong, and the next deployment is a surprise. It may undo the manual change in the middle of the day. Or it may fail because the real state no longer fits.

- **Change the file, not the resource.** The pipeline applies it.
- **Allow emergencies, then record them.** If a manual change is unavoidable, the same person opens a pull request that makes the file match, the same day.
- **Look for drift on a schedule.** Run the preview nightly against each environment. If it reports any change, something moved.

steps.title: In the pipeline
steps.text:
An infrastructure pipeline has the same shape as an application pipeline.

- **On a pull request:** check the files, run the preview against each environment, and show the output to the reviewer.
- **After the merge:** apply to development, then staging.
- **Production:** apply after approval, with the preview shown to the approver.

Two cautions are particular to infrastructure. The identity that applies it can create and delete resources, which is far more power than deploying an image needs. Keep it separate from the application's deploy identity and guard it more tightly. And treat any **delete** in a preview of production as a stop sign until a person has confirmed it is intended.

steps.title: A small rename
steps.text: A pull request renames the database resource in the description "for consistency". This is part of the preview for production.

steps.title: Exercise: bring an environment under control
steps.text:
A team has a production environment that was built by hand two years ago, and no staging. They want infrastructure as code. Put these steps in a sensible order and say why.

- Apply the description to production.
- Write a description that matches production as it is today.
- Build a staging environment from the description.
- Run the preview against production until it reports no changes.
- Remove people's rights to change production by hand.
- Add a nightly drift check.

steps.title: One possible answer
steps.text:
1. **Write a description that matches production as it is.** Change nothing yet. The aim is a true picture.
2. **Run the preview against production until it reports no changes.** Each difference it shows is a place where the file is wrong. Fix the file, not production.
3. **Build staging from the description.** This proves the description is complete: if staging does not work, something exists in production that the file does not mention.
4. **Apply the description to production.** With a clean preview, this changes nothing, and from now on the file is the source of truth.
5. **Add the nightly drift check.**
6. **Remove rights to change production by hand,** keeping an emergency route that is logged.

The order matters. Applying before the preview is clean would let the tool "correct" production to match an incomplete file.

questions.prompt: What does the second run do?

choices.text: Creates a second copy of everything
choices.feedback: That is what a script of create commands would attempt. A declarative tool compares first.

choices.text: Fails, because the resources already exist
choices.feedback: Existing resources that match the description are simply left as they are.

choices.text: Nothing, because reality already matches the description
choices.feedback: The tool finds no difference and makes no change. That is why applying on every merge is safe.

questions.prompt: What should the reviewer do?

choices.text: Stop the change: it would delete the production database
choices.feedback: To the tool, a new name is a new resource, and the old one is no longer described. The preview shows a delete and a create, which means an empty database. The name must stay, or the change needs a planned migration of the data.

choices.text: Approve it, since only a name changes
choices.feedback: The diff shows a name. The preview shows what the tool will actually do with it.

choices.text: Approve it, and restore from backup afterwards
choices.feedback: That is a planned outage with data loss, for a cosmetic change.

lessons.title: Know whether it is working
lessons.intro: A pipeline exists to make delivery faster and safer. This module covers how to tell whether it does: four numbers that describe a delivery process, a few that describe the pipeline itself, and the signals that reveal a bad release in minutes.

steps.title: Opinions and numbers
steps.text:
Ask a team whether its delivery is good and you get feelings. "Releases are stressful." "The pipeline is slow." "We break things a lot." These are worth hearing, and impossible to track or compare.

A small set of numbers turns the feeling into something you can watch change. The aim is not a score. It is to see whether last quarter's improvement actually improved anything, and where the next one should go.

steps.title: Four numbers
steps.text:
Research on software delivery settled on four measures. Two describe speed, and two describe stability.

| Measure | Question it answers |
| --- | --- |
| **Deployment frequency** | How often do we release to production? |
| **Lead time for changes** | How long from a commit to that commit running in production? |
| **Change failure rate** | What share of releases cause a failure that needs fixing or rolling back? |
| **Time to restore service** | When a release does fail, how long until users are served properly again? |

The finding that surprises people is that speed and stability are **not** a trade-off. Teams that release more often tend to fail less and recover faster. The cause is batch size: a small release has less in it to go wrong and less to search when it does.

steps.title: Releasing rarely, to be safe
steps.text: A team releases once a month "to be careful". Each release contains about 200 changes. One release in three causes an incident, and incidents take hours to resolve.

steps.title: Where the numbers come from
steps.text:
All four can be worked out from records the pipeline already keeps.

- **Deployment frequency:** count the successful production deployments each week.
- **Lead time:** for each deployment, the time from the oldest commit in it to the deployment finishing. Use the middle value over a month, since a few stuck changes distort an average.
- **Change failure rate:** deployments followed by a rollback, a fix released in a hurry, or an incident, divided by all deployments.
- **Time to restore:** from when the failure began to when service was normal again.

The first two need only the deployment record. The second two need each rollback and incident to be linked to the release that caused it, which is a habit worth starting early.

steps.title: Numbers about the pipeline itself
steps.text:
The four measures describe the outcome. A few more describe the tool.

| Measure | Why it matters |
| --- | --- |
| Time for a pull request's checks | This is what every developer waits for, many times a day. |
| Share of runs on `main` that pass | A low share means `main` is often broken. |
| Share of failures that pass on a rerun | This is the flaky rate. It should be close to zero. |
| Time waiting for a runner | Queueing is delay that no one sees in the step timings. |
| Time `main` stays red after it breaks | How quickly the team notices and reverts. |

Look at the slow end, not only the typical run. If one run in ten takes three times as long, that is the one people remember.

steps.title: Knowing a release is bad
steps.text:
The pipeline's checks end when the release finishes. The first minutes after it are when a bad release shows itself, and something has to be looking.

Four signals cover most failures: the **error rate**, the **response time**, the **amount of traffic**, and how **full** the service's resources are. A release that doubles the error rate or halves the traffic is wrong, whatever the tests said.

- **Mark deployments on the graphs.** A line at the moment of each release makes "did this start with the deploy?" a glance.
- **Put the version in every log line.** Then errors can be counted by version.
- **Alert on what users feel.** An alert for a rising error rate is acted on. An alert for a busy processor at 3 a.m. is ignored.

steps.title: Letting the pipeline decide
steps.text:
The next step is for the pipeline to watch those signals itself. After a release, it waits a few minutes, compares the error rate with the rate before, and rolls back without being asked if the release made things worse.

This is powerful and has a precondition: the signals must be trustworthy. An automatic rollback driven by a noisy measurement will undo good releases, and people will switch it off.

Get there in steps. First, a person watches after each release. Then the pipeline posts the comparison and a person decides. Only then does the pipeline act alone.

steps.title: A number became a goal
steps.text: Six months after a team began reporting its four measures to management.

steps.title: Exercise: work out the four
steps.text:
From the month of records below, work out each of the four measures. Then say which one you would work on first.

| Release | Oldest commit to production | Outcome |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | 6 days | Fine |
| 2 | 9 days | Rolled back, restored in 3 hours |
| 3 | 5 days | Fine |
| 4 | 12 days | Hurried fix, restored in 5 hours |

steps.title: One possible answer
steps.text:
- **Deployment frequency:** 4 a month, about one a week.
- **Lead time:** the middle of 5, 6, 9 and 12 days is 7.5 days.
- **Change failure rate:** 2 of 4, so 50 percent.
- **Time to restore:** 3 and 5 hours, so about 4 hours.

Work on **lead time and frequency first**, which are one problem. A week between a commit and production means changes pile up into large releases, and large releases are why half of them fail. Releasing each merged change by itself would shrink every release.

Second, time to restore. Three hours for a rollback says that going back is not one practised step. With kept artifacts and a rollback workflow it should be minutes.

questions.prompt: What is the most likely effect of releasing weekly instead?

choices.text: Four times as many incidents
choices.feedback: That assumes each release is as risky as before. Each would hold a quarter of the changes.

choices.text: Smaller releases that fail less often and are quicker to diagnose
choices.feedback: Fifty changes go wrong less often than two hundred, and when one does there is far less to search. Releasing more often lowers the risk of each release.

choices.text: No change, since the same changes ship in the end
choices.feedback: The same changes ship, in smaller groups. The size of the group is what decides how often a release fails and how long a failure takes to trace.

questions.prompt: What went wrong?

choices.text: The measures were turned into targets, so people changed the numbers and not the work
choices.feedback: Splitting one release into five and declining to record incidents improve the figures and nothing else. Measures are for the team to learn from. Once they are used to judge people, they stop describing reality.

choices.text: The team measured the wrong four things
choices.feedback: The measures are sound. The way they were used is the problem.

choices.text: Deployment frequency should not be measured
choices.feedback: It is a useful signal when nobody is rewarded for inflating it.

lessons.title: Review and design a pipeline
lessons.intro: This last module has no new ideas. It asks you to use the earlier ones together, twice: first to review a pipeline that works and has many faults, then to design a pipeline for a small service from a description. Do each exercise on paper before reading the answer.

steps.title: How to review a pipeline
steps.text:
A pipeline that goes green can still be slow, unsafe, or impossible to undo. Read one with a fixed list of questions.

| Question | Module |
| --- | --- |
| What starts it, and can unreviewed code start a deployment? | Triggers, Secrets |
| Do the cheap checks run first, and can a failure be hidden? | Stages |
| Is anything downloaded or run that need not be? | Speed |
| Is the artifact built once and named permanently? | Artifacts |
| Does it pass through environments with a gate before production? | Environments |
| How does it sign in, and how much can it reach? | Secrets |
| Is the new version checked before users reach it? | Deploy |
| Can the previous version be restored in minutes? | Rollback |
| Can old and new code both run against the database? | Database |
| Is shared logic called at a pinned version? | Reuse |
| Is the infrastructure described and previewed? | Infrastructure |
| Would anyone notice a bad release? | Measure |

steps.title: Review: one workflow
steps.text:
This workflow is a small team's whole pipeline. It works: changes reach production. Find as many problems as you can. There are at least twelve. For each, say what could go wrong.

Then continue.

steps.title: The most urgent one
steps.text: You have read the workflow above. The repository is public, and anyone can open a pull request.

steps.title: Review: what is wrong
steps.text:
**Who can deploy**

1. `on: [push, pull_request]` deploys from every branch and every pull request. Unreviewed code reaches production.
2. No `environment`, so no approval and no scoped secrets.
3. No `concurrency`. Two runs can deploy at once and finish in the wrong order.

**Access**

4. A stored, long-lived admin credential. Use federated identity with rights over one resource group.
5. An unknown third-party action at `@master`, handed that credential.
6. No `permissions:` block.
7. The commit message is pasted into a script. Its author chooses what runs.

**Checks**

8. The 40-minute end-to-end suite runs before lint. Cheap checks should come first.
9. `npm test || true` can never fail. Unit test failures are hidden.
10. `npm install` may fetch versions other than the ones tested. Use `npm ci`, with a cache.

**Artifact and release**

11. The image is tagged `latest`. No release can be identified or restored.
12. Build and deploy are one job, straight to production. There is no staging and no promotion.
13. No smoke test and no slot. The job ends when the command is accepted.
14. The migration renames and drops columns in the same release as the code, directly on production.

A repaired design is below, as an outline. Each box is a job or a reusable workflow from an earlier module.

steps.title: Design: a pipeline for a notes service
steps.text:
A team of four is building a notes service. Design its delivery pipeline. You do not need to write the files. Decide, and give reasons.

- The service is a container image, deployed to Azure App Service with a second slot.
- It has a PostgreSQL database with migrations.
- There are development, staging and production environments.
- Unit tests take 2 minutes, integration tests 5 minutes, end-to-end tests 30 minutes.
- The team wants to release several times a day.

Decide: the triggers, the order of the checks, where the image is built and how it is named, how it moves between environments, how the pipeline signs in, how a release is checked, how it is rolled back, how migrations are handled, and what is measured.

steps.title: One decision
steps.text: In your design, a change has been merged, built as `notes:git-5b3e9aa`, and tested in staging. It is now to go to production.

steps.title: Design: one possible answer
steps.text:
**Triggers.** Checks on `pull_request`, with newer commits cancelling older runs. Build and deploy to development and staging on `push` to `main`. Production by `workflow_dispatch` with the tag as input. One concurrency group for each environment, never cancelled.

**Checks.** On the pull request: lint and type check first, then unit and integration tests side by side, about 6 minutes in all. After the merge: a few end-to-end smoke tests against staging. Nightly: the full 30-minute suite, with failures sent to the team.

**Artifact.** Built once, after the merge, tagged `git-<commit>`, pushed to the registry. Nothing later builds.

**Environments.** Development and staging automatically, in turn. Production after one approval from someone other than the person who started it. Each environment has its own variables and its own identity.

**Access.** Federated identity, no stored keys, rights over one resource group each. `permissions` set to the minimum. Outside actions pinned to commit identifiers.

**Release.** Deploy to the idle slot, smoke test it, swap, smoke test production, swap back on failure.

**Rollback.** A manual workflow that needs no approval: swap back within minutes of a release, or deploy an earlier tag. The deployment record names the previous tag.

**Database.** Additive migrations only, run as a job before the new code, in staging first. Renames and removals go through expand and contract over several releases.

**Measures.** The four delivery numbers from the deployment record, the time of the pull request checks, and the error rate with a marker for each deployment.

steps.title: Where to go next
steps.text:
This course used one pipeline tool and one cloud so that its examples could be compared. The file formats differ elsewhere. The decisions do not.

The habits that carry over:

- Merge small changes often, and keep the shared branch releasable.
- Run cheap checks first, and never let a failure be hidden or ignored.
- Build once, name it permanently, and promote the same artifact.
- Give the pipeline short-lived access to as little as possible.
- Check a new version before users reach it, and keep the way back open.
- Change the database in steps that the previous version can live with.
- Describe infrastructure in files, and read the preview.
- Measure, to learn and not to judge.

questions.prompt: Which problem should be fixed first?

choices.text: The end-to-end tests run before lint
choices.feedback: That wastes time on every run. It exposes nothing.

choices.text: The image is tagged `latest`
choices.feedback: That makes rollback impossible, which matters a great deal. It still needs someone inside the team to trigger harm.

choices.text: Any pull request deploys its code to production with admin credentials
choices.feedback: A stranger can open a pull request that changes the build or the tests, and the workflow will run it with a credential that controls the cloud account, then deploy the result. Limit the deploy to `main` and remove the stored credential before anything else.

questions.prompt: What does the production workflow do with that tag?

choices.text: Points production's idle slot at the existing image, checks it, and swaps
choices.feedback: Nothing is rebuilt. The image that staging tested is the one that runs, and the slot keeps the old version ready for a swap back.

choices.text: Checks out the commit and builds a fresh image for production
choices.feedback: A second build is a different artifact, which staging never tested.

choices.text: Retags it as `latest` and restarts production
choices.feedback: A moving tag cannot say what is running or what ran before, and a restart gives no check before users arrive.

good.code:
PULL REQUEST            (cancel older runs, read-only permissions)

    lint | type check  -->  unit | integration          about 6 min

  PUSH TO MAIN            (one at a time for each environment)

    publish image  tracker:git-<commit>     built once, npm ci, cached
          |
    deploy development  -->  smoke test
          |
    migrate staging (additive only)  -->  deploy staging  -->  smoke test

  MANUAL: PROMOTE TO PRODUCTION      input: tag

    approval (environment: production, federated identity)
          |
    migrate (additive only)
          |
    deploy to slot "next"  -->  smoke test  -->  swap  -->  smoke test
                                                   |
                                         on failure: swap back

  MANUAL: ROLL BACK                  no approval, swap or earlier tag
